# Using Contradictions in Interiority

February 25, 2026

15

![](https://bigpulp.com/slushpile/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/writing-34-696x418.jpg "writing 34")

Image by Angela Yuriko Smith from Pixabay

In a new post, C.S. Lakin continues her exploration of how contradictions can create tension, this time focusing on interiority. “These techniques are especially powerful because they require no additional plot considerations,” she writes. “They can work in quiet scenes, transitional moments, and conversations that appear ordinary on the surface but are anything but.”

Characters naturally have contradictions. They want something but are afraid to chase it. They say one thing and act in the opposite way. “Microtension emerges when the narrative homes in on that division rather than rushing past it,” Lakin notes. Often, interiority is used to explain or justify, but uncertainty creates tension. “When a character misunderstands her own emotions, resists acknowledging a desire, or acts against what she believes she wants, the reader leans in,” she writes. “We sense the story knows more than the character does.”

What might that look like? A character may get bad news and feel both relief and ashamed at feeling relieved. She might say she doesn’t care about something, but act in a way that suggests she does. He might be decisive on the outside, torn by doubt on the inside. When these feelings coexist, the contradiction creates an underlying tension.

This also applies to physical reactions. A character may feel tense or frightened without knowing why. They may feel irrationally angry or sad without a surface reason. Rather than explaining the contradiction, let it linger. They may act in a way that contradicts who they think they are. “When who they think they are comes into quiet conflict with what they’re doing, microtension deepens into character development,” Lakin writes.

Contradictions also arise when characters act against their desires or interests. “These moments of self-betrayal often stem from fear, habit, or self-protection rather than logic,” Lakin says. “A character may reach for distance when they crave connection, soften their voice when they want to lash out, or make a choice that preserves the status quo while quietly resenting themselves for it. The contradiction between desire and action creates tension because the reader can see the cost even when the character cannot.” These moments are subtle, because the action may appear reasonable on the surface, while the reader can sense something is off.

Characters may also misinterpret what they’re feeling. “When a character mislabels fear as anger, desire as curiosity, or grief as indifference, the story gains friction,” Laking writes, adding that the contradiction should not be resolved quickly, but remain a pressure point. “As long as the character remains invested in their false explanation, every thought and decision is slightly off balance,” she explains. “The longer the misinterpretation holds, the more tension accumulates—not through confusion but dramatic irony.”
